title: Bob Dylan and the folk protest
subject: art
description: From Greenwich Village to the Nobel, Bob Dylan transforms folk song into political poetry, then into electric rock.

hero.hook: A guitar, a harmonica, and American song becomes literature.

blocks.text: **Bob Dylan**, born Robert Zimmerman in **1941** in Minnesota, is one of the most influential figures of 20th century song. Prophet of protest, then electric poet, he refuses to stay in a single box.
In **2016**, the Swedish Academy awarded him the **Nobel Prize for Literature**. For the first time, a rock songwriter is recognized as a great writer in the English language.

sections.title: Greenwich Village and the legacy of Woody Guthrie

blocks.text: In January **1961**, at age 19, Zimmerman left the cold of the Midwest for **New York**. He has already chosen the name Bob Dylan. His idol: the folk singer **Woody Guthrie**, voice of the workers and the oppressed, then hospitalized. Dylan wants to encounter this American authenticity.

He settled in **Greenwich Village**, a bohemian neighborhood in Manhattan. This is the heart of , this movement which rediscovers traditional songs to make them a lever of social criticism. Dylan scours cafes, absorbs blues, country and gospel, and also discovers poetry and . [[folk revival]] [[Beat Generation]]

blocks.caption: Greenwich Village in the 1960s: cafes, guitars and protests.

blocks.text: Spotted for his phrasing and his raw harmonica, he signed with  at the end of **1961**. The legend begins. [[Columbia Records]]
In his early days, Dylan invented his biography: he claimed to have fled a circus or traveled with carnivals, to forge an aura of outsider.

sections.title: The protest song and the March on Washington

blocks.text: In **1963**, the album *The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan* changed everything. *Blowin' in the Wind* becomes an anthem. Dylan uses : simple melodies, messages about racism, war and nuclear fear. [[Music as a political tool]]

In August **1963**, he sang at the **March on Washington** for civil rights, in front of **250,000** people, just before **Martin Luther King**'s speech. However, he is already beginning to reject the role of “spokesperson for a generation”. His texts become more surreal, more personal.

blocks.caption: August 1963: the March on Washington, a key moment in civil rights.

blocks.text: The same year, television producers failed him at an audition: they found that he sang too out of tune.

In July **1965**, at the Newport Folk Festival, Dylan took the stage with an electric . Part of the purist public boos him: electricity would be a commercial betrayal. In reality, it was the birth of folk-rock. [[Fender Stratocaster]]

blocks.caption: Newport 1965: Dylan turns on the electricity, and an era changes.

blocks.text: A founding trilogy follows: *Bringing It All Back Home*, *Highway 61 Revisited*, *Blonde on Blonde*. *Like a Rolling Stone* is shattering radio formats. Dylan no longer only accuses society: he explores disillusionment and the psyche, with a verbal verve unprecedented at the top of the charts.
Newport's Stratocaster was lost for 47 years, forgotten on a plane, then sold at auction for nearly $1 million in 2013.

sections.title: From the Never Ending Tour to the Nobel

blocks.text: After a motorcycle accident in **1966**, Dylan constantly reinvented himself: country, gospel, standards. His influence touches **John Lennon**, **Jimi Hendrix** and generations of authors. The Nobel Prize for **2016** seals the debate: song lyrics can be great literature.
